newsitem.title: USA: US, Japan want stable dlr/yen rate-Japan officials.
newsitem.headline: US, Japan want stable dlr/yen rate-Japan officials.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The United States and Japan basically see eye-to-eye on currencies and would prefer not to see any wide swings in the dollar/yen rate in either direction, Japanese officials said Thursday.
The officials, who declined to be named, said Washington and Tokyo were more or less satisfied with the current constellation of exchange rates between the two countries.
After rising some 40 percent against the Japanese yen over the past 18 months, the dollar has recently shown signs of stabilizing. It opened in New York Thursday at 112.80/90 yen.

Speaking in a television interview in Tokyo on Thursday, senior Japanese Ministry of Finance (MOF) official Eisuke Sakakibara said that the United States, Japan and Europe all welcomed currency moves over the past year.
Sakakibara, the director general of MOF's International Finance Bureau, denied Tokyo has a target zone for the yen.

The official, who helped engineer the dollar's meteoric rise from a record low of 79.75 yen in April 1995, rocked currency markets last month when he seemed to suggest that the U.S. currency's climb was coming to an end. At that time, the dollar was trading just below 115 yen.

For its part, the United States has shied away from trying to micro-manage the currency market, with Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin content to repeat his mantra that the Clinton administration prefers a strong dollar.
European policymakers have not been so reticent, with senior officials from France and Germany recently repeatedly calling for not just a strong dollar, but a stronger one.
Japanese officials said they are watching the Europeans' concerted campaign to talk the dollar up against their currencies for signs that might upset Tokyo's desire for a stable dollar/yen rate.
So far, that does not seem to have happened, as the dollar has risen in recent days against the German mark but basically held steady against the yen.
Japan itself has been accused by U.S. manufacturing companies of trying to manipulate the yen lower to increase the competitiveness of its products on world markets.

Rubin told Reuters last week that he did not know whether Tokyo was manipulating the currency market. But he also declined to say whether the United States had privately called Japan to task for doing just that.
Deputy finance ministers from the Group of Seven -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- are likely to discuss currency and other issues in Paris next week.

The G7 deputies will be in Paris for a December 9-10 meeting of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development's Working Party Three -- senior officials from industrial nations who meet regularly to take stock of the world economy.
Japanese officials said their country's economy is picking up -- but U.S. officials do not seem so certain.
Rubin told Reuters last week that he was unsure about the Japanese economy's staying power and said the authorities there needed to be "watchful" as their past budgetary stimulus is phased out.
Japan is set to raise its consumption tax in April to five percent from three percent.

Rubin said that European nations too needed to be "watchful" about the course of their economies and should try to put in place policies that promote solid growth with low inflation. European growth faltered earlier this year, although it has recently shown some signs of picking up.
At their meeting next week in Paris, G7 deputies may also finalize plans for a gathering of their finance ministers sometime in mid-February.
